prediction: The appellant was the husband of the deceased, Subhadramma. They were married for approximately one and a half years before the incident. About three months prior to the incident, the deceased gave birth to a female child at the appellant's house in Cherlopalle. Following customary practice, the deceased and the child were taken to her maternal home in Krishna Kalva, about 25 miles away, after nine days. The appellant frequently visited his wife at her maternal home. Approximately one and a half months after the birth, the appellant requested his mother-in-law and brother-in-law to send his wife back to his house. They refused, stating she needed to recover for five months. On December 18, 1972, the appellant again requested his mother-in-law to send his wife, accompanied by an elderly villager, P.W. 8. The mother-in-law, P.W. 2, reiterated the refusal. That evening, the appellant returned to the house. All family members, including the appellant, the deceased, her brother (P.W. 1), her mother (P.W. 2), and her grandmother (P.W. 3), slept in a single room. During the night, P.Ws. 1, 2, and 3 were awakened by the deceased crying 'Amma'. Upon waking, they saw the appellant sitting beside the deceased with a knife in his hand. The deceased was bleeding profusely from the left side of her chest. P.W. 1 stepped on the appellant's hand, causing him to drop the knife, which was picked up by P.W. 3. Neighbors (P.Ws. 4, 5, 6) arrived upon hearing the cries, apprehended the appellant, and tied him to a pole. P.W. 1 reported the incident to the Village Munsif, P.W. 9, who prepared a report and forwarded the blood-stained knife (M.O. 1) to the police. The police registered the First Information Report on December 19, 1972, and arrested the appellant, who had injuries on his person. The post-mortem examination revealed a stab wound 6 cm below the left armpit, passing through the third intercostal space and the upper lobe of the left lung in an upward and medial direction. The Additional Sessions Judge acquitted the appellant, finding the prosecution evidence discrepant and holding that two views were possible, thus granting the benefit of doubt. The High Court of Andhra Pradesh reversed the acquittal, convicting the appellant under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentencing him to life imprisonment. The appellant filed a criminal appeal under Section 2(a) of the Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction Act, 1882. The question before the Court was Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the Sessions Judge's order of acquittal and convicting the appellant under Section 302 IPC, considering the appellant's contention that two views of the evidence were possible and he was entitled to the benefit of doubt. Held: Appeal dismissed: The appeal is dismissed, and the conviction and sentence of the appellant under Section 302 IPC by the High Court are affirmed. The Court considered Indian Penal Code: Defines the offence of murder for which the appellant was convicted. Sanwat Singh & Ors. vs State of Rajasthan (Relied on): Established that appellate courts have the right to review the entire evidence and come to their own conclusion, abandoning the rigid formula of 'substantial and compelling reasons' for interfering with acquittals. Sheo Swarup vs Emperor (Relied on): Privy Council principles reaffirmed regarding the appellate court's power to review evidence. Ramabhupala Reddy & Ors. v The State of A.P. (Relied on): Cited for the principle that if two reasonable conclusions can be reached, the appellate court should not disturb the trial court's finding. Benefit of Reasonable Doubt: Clarifies that the benefit of doubt applies only to reasonable doubts, not to fanciful, remote, or airy possibilities. A view in favor of the accused must be as nearly reasonably probable as the view against him. Miller vs Minister of Pensions (Referred): Quoted to distinguish 'proof beyond reasonable doubt' from 'proof beyond a shadow of a doubt'. Khem Karan & Ors. vs State of U.P. & Anr. (Relied on): Observed that mere or remote possibilities cannot form the foundation of acquittal if there is fairly credible testimony. Applying those rules, On Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the Sessions Judge's order of acquittal and convicting the appellant under Section 302 IPC, considering the appellant's contention that two views of the evidence were possible and he was entitled to the benefit of doubt, the Sessions Judge acquitted the appellant based on minor discrepancies in witness testimony and the possibility of two views of the evidence. The High Court reversed this, finding the discrepancies trivial and the prosecution evidence credible. The legal standard for interfering with an acquittal, as per Sanwat Singh and Sheo Swarup, allows the appellate court to review the entire evidence and reach its own conclusion. The principle of 'benefit of doubt' requires that the alternative view in favor of the accused be reasonably probable, not merely fanciful or remote. The discrepancies cited by the Sessions Judge (e.g., who woke up first, location of lantern) are minor and do not undermine the core credibility of P.Ws. 1, 2, and 3, who saw the appellant with the knife next to the bleeding deceased. The medical evidence shows a stab wound 6 cm below the left armpit, directed upward and medial through the lung. The appellant's defense version claims the deceased was stabbed while standing and intervening between the appellant and P.W. 1. The nature, location, and upward direction of the injury are medically inconsistent with the defense version of a standing victim. The medical evidence supports the prosecution version that the deceased was lying on her right side when the injury was inflicted. The appellant's claim that P.W. 3's testimony was improved is rejected; even if her specific observation of the gesture is disregarded, it does not invalidate the testimony of the other witnesses. The motive is established by the appellant's frustration over the refusal of the deceased's family to send her back to his house. The Sessions Judge allowed fanciful doubts to override creditworthy evidence. Since the prosecution version is reasonably probable and supported by medical evidence, while the defense version is medically improbable, there is no reasonable doubt in favor of the accused. The High Court was justified in interfering to prevent the administration of justice from being brought to ridicule. The High Court was justified in reversing the acquittal and convicting the appellant, as the prosecution evidence was credible, the defense version was medically improbable, and the benefit of doubt does not apply to fanciful possibilities.
reference_summary:
The appellant was charged with the offence of committing the murder of his wife.
The trial court acquitted him on the ground that the prosecution had failed to establish any motive for the offence, that the evidence of the prosecution witnesses was discrepant, conflicting and improbable and that when two views were possible on the basis of two divergent versions given by the prosecution and the defence, the benefit of doubt should be given to the accused.
The High Court reversed the order of acquittal and convicted and sentenced the appellant to imprisonment for life on the view that the trial court had magnified the importance to be attached to the discrepancies which were of a minor nature In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that in all cases where two views of the evidence were possible the accused was entitled to the benefit of doubt arising from the two views and that on this principle the High Court should not have interfered with the order of acquittal merely because another view was also possible.
Dismissing the appeal: ^ HELD : (1) Where the trial court allows itself to be beset with fanciful doubts, rejects creditworthy evidence for slender reasons and takes a view of the evidence which is but barely possible, it is the obvious duty of the High Court to interfere in the interest of justice, lest the administration of justice be brought to ridicule.
[370D] (2) After the decision of this Court in Sanwat Singh vs State of Rajasthan ; this Court has consistently recognised the right of the appellate court to review the entire evidence and to come to its own conclusion bearing in mind the considerations mentioned by the Privy Council in Sheo Swarup vs Emperor (61 T.A. 389).
Occasionally phrases like "manifestly illegal", "grossly unjust have been used to describe the orders of acquittal which warrant interference.
But such expressions have been used more as flourishes of language to emphasise the reluctance of the appellate court to interfere with an order of acquittal than to curtail the power of the appellate court to review the entire evidence and to come to its own conclusion.
In two other cases it has been held that to the principles laid down in Sanwat Singh 's case may added the further principle that if two 364 reasonable conclusions could be reached on the basis of the evidence on record the appellate court should not disturb the finding of the trial court.
This principle stems out of the fundamental principle of our criminal jurisprudence that the accused is entitled to the benefit of any reasonable doubt.
If two reasonably probable and evenly balanced views of the evidence are possible one must necessarily concede the existence of a reasonable doubt.
But fanciful and remote possibilities must be left out of account.
To entitle an accused person to the benefit of a doubt arising from the possibility of duality of views, the possible view in favour of the accused must be as nearly reasonably probable as that against him.
If the preponderance of probability is all one way, a bare possibility of another view will not entitle the accused to claim the benefit of any doubt.
It is, therefore essential that, any view of the evidence in favour of the accused must be reasonable even as any doubt, the benefit of which an accused person may claim, must be reasonable.
A reasonable doubt does not mean some light, airy, insubstantial doubt that may flit through the mind of a Judge about almost anything at any time or other, it does not mean a doubt begotten by sympathy out of reluctance to convict, it means a real doubt, a doubt founded upon reason.
"Proof beyond a reasonable doubt" does not mean proof beyond a shadow of doubt The law would fail to protect the community if it admitted fanciful possibilities to deflect the course of justice.
If the evidence is so strong against a man be to leave only a remote possibility in his favour which can be dismissed with the sentence, "of course it is possible but not in the least probable," the case is proved beyond reasonable doubt but nothing short of that will suffice.

vs The State of A.P., AIR 1971 SC 460, Bhim Singh Rup Singh vs State of Maharashtra, AIR 1974 SC 286, Miller vs Minister of Pensions, [1947] 2 All.

vs State of U.P. & Anr., referred to.

prediction: The dispute concerns the allotment of four acres of land, known as Begumbari land, located adjacent to the Alipore Zoological Garden in Calcutta, to the Taj Group of Hotels for the construction of a Five Star Hotel. The Begumbari land was originally granted to the Zoological Garden in 1880 on terms that it be used for acclimatization and that it be restored to the Government if required. In 1980, the Government of West Bengal sought to promote tourism by constructing Five Star Hotels in Calcutta and identified the Begumbari land as a potential site after other locations were found unsuitable. The land was used by the Zoo for fodder cultivation, a dumping ground, a burial ground, and essential facilities including a hospital, operation theater, and quarantine areas. The Public Undertakings Committee, the Managing Committee of the Zoo, and the Director of the Zoo initially raised objections regarding the displacement of these facilities and the potential impact on migratory birds and ecological balance. The Government addressed these objections by assuring the relocation of essential zoo facilities to adjacent land and providing matching grants, which were incorporated into the lease deed. The Managing Committee of the Zoo withdrew its objections after receiving assurances from the Chief Minister regarding the reconstruction of facilities. The Cabinet approved the lease to the Taj Group in September 1981, and possession was handed over in January 1982, subject to the execution of a lease deed. The lease deed stipulated that the Taj Group would reconstruct the essential structures on adjacent land at its own cost, which it did, spending Rs. 30 lakhs. The appellants, citizens and zoo members, filed a writ petition challenging the allotment as arbitrary, ecologically damaging, and procedurally flawed for not inviting tenders. The Single Judge and the Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court dismissed the writ petition, upholding the Government's decision. The appellants appealed to the Supreme Court under Article 136 of the Constitution. The question before the Court was Whether the Government of West Bengal acted arbitrarily or failed to apply its mind to relevant ecological and administrative considerations in allotting the Begumbari land to the Taj Group of Hotels; and Whether the Government was obligated to invite tenders or hold a public auction for the lease of the land, or whether direct negotiation with the Taj Group was justified under the circumstances; and Whether the construction of the hotel would adversely affect the ecological balance, specifically the migratory birds and the welfare of the zoo animals. Held: Appeal dismissed: The appeal was dismissed, affirming the judgments of the High Court and upholding the Government's decision to lease the Begumbari land to the Taj Group of Hotels. The Court considered Constitution of India: The court considered this Directive Principle as binding on the Court to ensure the State protects and improves the environment and safeguards wildlife. Constitution of India: The court considered this Fundamental Duty requiring citizens to protect the natural environment and have compassion for living creatures. Bengal Public Parks Act, 1904: The court examined this Act to determine if it vested property rights in the Zoo Managing Committee, concluding it only regulated park management and did not vest title. West Bengal Land Management Manual, 1977: The court considered whether these rules mandating public auction/tenders applied, holding they did not apply to socio-economic objectives like tourism development. R.D. Shetty v. International Airport Authority (Relied on): Relied on for the principle that government contracts must be fair, non-discriminatory, and not arbitrary, but that departures from norms are valid if based on rational principles. Kasturi Lal Laxmi Reddy v. State of Jammu & Kashmir (Relied on): Relied on for the principle that the State is not bound to obtain the highest market price if other public interest considerations (like promoting industry/tourism) justify a different approach. Mohinder Singh Gill v. Central Election Commission (Distinguished): The court distinguished this case, noting it involved a statutory functionary where reasons cannot be supplemented later, whereas the present case involved commercial negotiations where the entire course of events must be viewed. Principle of Non-Arbitrariness in Government Action: The court applied the principle that government action must not be arbitrary, irrational, or irrelevant, and must be informed by public interest. Applying those rules, On Whether the Government of West Bengal acted arbitrarily or failed to apply its mind to relevant ecological and administrative considerations in allotting the Begumbari land to the Taj Group of Hotels, the Court examines whether the executive decision was taken after considering relevant factors and excluding irrelevant ones. The record shows a two-year decision-making process involving Cabinet memoranda, inter-departmental notes, and negotiations. Objections regarding the displacement of zoo facilities were raised by the Public Undertakings Committee, the Managing Committee, and the Director of the Zoo. The Government addressed these objections by assuring the relocation of essential services to adjacent land and providing matching grants. The Managing Committee withdrew its objection after receiving assurances from the Chief Minister. The lease deed explicitly mandated the reconstruction of essential structures by the lessee, which was implemented. The Court finds that the Government applied its mind to all relevant considerations, including the needs of the Zoo, and did not act arbitrarily. The Government of West Bengal did not act arbitrarily and duly considered all relevant ecological and administrative factors before granting the lease. On Whether the Government was obligated to invite tenders or hold a public auction for the lease of the land, or whether direct negotiation with the Taj Group was justified under the circumstances, the appellants argue that the Government violated the Land Management Manual by not inviting tenders. The Court distinguishes between disposal of public property for revenue maximization and allotment for specific socio-economic objectives like tourism. Precedents establish that the State is not bound to obtain the highest market price if other public interest considerations justify a different approach. Constructing a Five Star Hotel requires specific expertise and financial capacity, limiting the pool of eligible bidders. Only two major hotel groups came forward, and negotiations with one did not fructify. The Court holds that inviting tenders was impractical and unnecessary given the specialized nature of the project. Direct negotiation with the Taj Group was rational, non-discriminatory, and served the public interest of boosting tourism. The Government was justified in negotiating directly with the Taj Group without inviting tenders or holding a public auction. On Whether the construction of the hotel would adversely affect the ecological balance, specifically the migratory birds and the welfare of the zoo animals, the Court considers the constitutional mandate under Articles 48A and 51A(g) to protect the environment. The appellants contend that the hotel would disturb migratory birds and ecological balance. The Court examines assurances and technical details provided by the Taj Group and independent experts. The hotel is designed as a 'garden hotel' with a maximum height of 75 feet, lower than surrounding high-rises. Expert ornithologists confirmed that the height and location would not interfere with bird flight paths. The Taj Group agreed to use subdued lighting and plant trees to improve local ecology. The removal of the dumping ground and burial ground is viewed as an environmental improvement. The Court finds no credible evidence that the hotel would cause significant harm to the zoo animals or migratory birds. The construction of the hotel is not likely to cause significant adverse effects on the ecological balance, migratory birds, or zoo animals.

There is in Calcutta, a Zoological garden located in Alipore, now almost the heart of Calcutta, on either side of Belvedere Road, one of Calcutta 's main arterial roads, fortynine acres of land on one side and eight acres on the other.
The main zoo is in the fortynine acres block of land.
The said eight acres of land was outside the Zoological garden and separated from it by a 80 100 feet road and is also known as the Begumbari land.
The Begumbari land was given to the Zoological garden in '1880.
According to a letter written on July 7, 1880 by the Assistant Secretary to the Government of Bengal in the Public works Department to Mr. L. Schwandler, Honorary Secretary Zoological garden conveying the sanction of the Lt. Governor for the transfer of the Begumbari land to the charge of the Committee of the Zoological Garden, on the terms agreed to by the Committee in their letter dated April 23, 1880, the conditions of the transfer were: "(i) that the land is to be used for the purpose of acclimatization only; (ii) that Carnivors are not to be kept on any part of it, on any account; (iii) that the grounds are to be kept clear and neat; (iv) that the land must be restored to the government if hereafter required, the Zoological Garden Committee being reimbursed for any expenditure they may have incurred in building there." In this eight acres of land there are some old buildings and the vacant land was used for fodder cultivation,for raising flower nursery, as a sumping ground for huge garbages and as burial ground for dead animals.
In January, 1979, the Director General of Tourism Gov ernment of India addressed a letter to the Chief Secretary Government of West Bengal conveying the Resolution of the Tourism conference which was presided over by the Union Minister of Tourism and attended by several State Ministers and requesting that land in good location may be made avail able for construction of hotels in a drive to encourage tourism.
In May, 1980, the Taj Group of Hotels came forward with a suggestion that they would be able to construct a Five Star Hotel.
On September 29, 1980 and November 29, 1980, there were two notes by the Secretary of the Metropol itan Development Department to the effect that the I.T.D.C. was interested in a property known as the Hastings House Properly and that the Taj Group of Hotels who considered the Hastings House properly unsuitable may be offered four acres out of the eight acres of Begumbari land.
On the same day the Taj Group of Hotels wrote to the Government of West Bengal stating that the proposed land could be seriously considered for construction of a hotel.
Thereafter, 225 the Chief Minister along with the Minister of Tourism and the Minister for Metropolitan Development visited the site accompanied by the Director of the Zoo to apparently knew about the proposal right from the start.
A note was then prepared by the Secretary, Metropolitan Development Depart ment and put up to the Chief Minister for his approval.
The Chief Minister approved the proposal and required it to be placed before the Cabinet.
On January 7, 1981 a memorandum was prepared for the consideration of the Cabinet explaining the need for the more Five Star Hotels in Calcutta and the benefits flowing out of the construction and establishment of such Five Star Hotels and suggesting the lease of Hast ings House Property to the I.T.D.C. Group and the Begumbari property to the Taj Group of Hotels.
In regard to the Begum bari property, it was stated: "From the property of the Zoological Gardens on the Belvedere Road it is possible to carve out about four acres of land currently used for dump ing garbage and also for growing grass for the elephants.

While adequate space can be made available for growing grass elsewhere in the same area.

1981 about the Zoo.

Two alternative financial arrangements were suggested.

The Metropolitan Development Department expressed a preference for the second alternative and suggested the constitution of a Committee.

Correspondence went on.
On June 5, 1981 a Committee of Secretaries was formally constituted.
In the meanwhile WEBCON, a West Bengal Government Consultancy Undertaking, was asked to examine the proposals and to advise the Govern ment.

right from the beginning wrote to the Secretary of Animal Husbandry and Veterinary Services Department stating his objections to the proposal to lease the land for construction of a hotel.

Taj Group suggested further modifications.

It was mentioned in the letter that the construction of the Hotel should not be started till the lease deed was executed and registered.

land in the extent of 288 square 228 meters out of the plot given to them was carved out and given hack for accommodating part of the reconstructed structures.

Five petitioners a Trade Unionist, two life members of the Zoo, two other bonafide residents of Greater Calcutta, all lovers of wild life filed a petition in public interest on 26.2.1982.
Initially the relief sought was primarily to restrain the Zoo authorities from giving effect to the two Resolutions dated January 7, 1982 and January 17, 1982 to hand over the four acres to the Animal Husbandry Department of the Government.

While the writ petition was pending in the High Court, Late Smt.
Indira Gandhi wrote a letter to Sri Jyothi Basu, the Chief Minister of West Bengal expressing the hope that he would not allow the Calcutta Zoo to suffer in any manner and would leave it intact.
The Chief Minister in his reply letter dated 21.8.82 pointed out that:(i) the four acres of land were agreed to be relinquished by the Committee of management of the Zoological Garden on condition that alter native arrangement were made for shifting the existing structures which were necessary for the Zoo from the plot in question to the adjacent plot; (ii) the plot in question was not a part of the Zoo Garden; (iii) till the existing struc tures are relocated on the adjacent land, the zoo would continue to get their services and facilities from the existing structures.
(iv) the hotel was not the only tall building since there existed many such residential buildings to which none raised an objection and that P&T Department are also constructing one such tall building; and (v) the lessee and their experts on wild life had assured them that in any case adequate precaution would be taken in regard to illumination of the hotel and the layout of the surrounding so that no disturbance would be caused to the flight path of the birds or animals.

Indira Gandhi wrote to Mr. Tata expressing her happiness that the hotel was not going to upset the Zoo animals and welcoming his offer to help the State Government to improve the Zoo 's facilities.
229 A learned Single Judge of the High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the West Bengal Government did not show any lack of awareness of the problem of environment ecology in granting the lease of land.
On appeal, a Division Bench confirmed the said judgment.
Hence the appeal by Special leave of the Court.
Dismissing the appeal, the Court, HELD: (Per Chinnappa Reddy J.) 1.1 Whenever a problem of ecology is brought before the Court, the Court is bound to bear in mind article 48 A of the Constitution the Directive Principle which enjoins that "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country, "and article 51A(g) Which proclaims it to be the fundamental duty of every citizen of India "to protect and improve the natural environment in cluding forest, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures.
" When the Court is called upon to give effect to the Directive Principle and the fundamental duty, the Court is not to shrug its shoulders and say that priorities are a matter of policy and so it is matter for the policy making authority.
The least that the court may do is to examine whether appropriate considera tions are borne in mind irrelevancies excluded.
In appropri ate cases, the Court may go further, but how much further must depend on the circumstances of the case.
The court may always give necessary directions.
However the Court will not attempt to nicely balance relevant considerations When the question involves the nice balancing of relevant considera tions, the court may feel justified in resigning itself to acceptance of the decision of the concerned authority.
If the Government is alive to the various considerations re quiring thought and deliberation and has arrived at a con scious decision after taking them into account, it may not be for the court to interfere in the absence of mala fides.
On the other hand, if relevant considerations are not borne in mind and irrelevant considerations influence the deci sion, the Court may interfere in order to prevent a likeli hood of prejudice to the public.
[242B F] 1.2 Applying the above guidelines to be followed when questions of ecology and environment are raised, it is clear that the facts and circumstances brought out by the appel lants do not justify an inference that the construction of the proposed hotel in the Begumbari land would interfere in any manner with the animals in the Zoo and the birds arriv ing at the zoo or otherwise disturb the ecology.
The pro posed hotel is a Garden hotel and there is perhaps every chance of the ecology and environment improving as a result of planting numerous trees all 230 around the proposed hotel and the removal of the burial ground and dumping ground for rubbish.
[263A B] 1.3 That the question of obstruction which may be caused to migratory birds did not go unnoticed by the government before the decision to lease the land was taken, is clear from the following: (i) the question of the migratory bird was first raised in the resolution of the Managing Committee dated June 11, 1981.

In this letter, the Chief Minister pointed out that there were already in existence a number of multistoreyed buildings all around the Zoological Garden, but there was no report that they had any adverse effect on the migratory birds or the animals.
He also pointed out that all precautions would be taken in the matter of illumination of the hotel and lay out of the surroundings so that no disturbance would be caused to the flight path of the birds or animals; (iii) Shri J.R.D. He further assured her that he had himself gone thoroughly in to the project with the special reference to the possible impact on the birds and the environment and had satisfied himself that project would not cause any disturbance to the birds or their free movement.
He pointed out that the four acre plot was not within the main Zoological Garden, but was separated from it by the Belvedere Road which was an impor tant thoroughfare in the city.
It was about 700 feet from the main part of the lake.
The hotel was proposed to be built away from the frontage of the plot in Belvedere Road and was to be a low rise structure, the highest point of which would not exceed 75 feet, far below the trajectory of the birds.

prediction: The respondent, a resident of the former Dholpur State, applied for and was granted an export permit for 15,000 maunds of chuni in June 1947. In connection with the permit, the respondent deposited Rs. 30,000 as advance export duty with the customs department of the former Dholpur State. The permit remained in force until December 2, 1947, but the respondent exported only 4,572 maunds and 20 seers of chuni due to market conditions and inability to secure railway wagons. The respondent claimed a refund of the proportionate export duty for the unexported quantity (10,427 maunds and 20 seers), amounting to Rs. 20,855, but the State refused to pay. The Matsya Union merged into the United State of Rajasthan in May 1949, which subsequently became the Part B State of Rajasthan on January 26, 1950, upon the commencement of the Constitution. The State of Rajasthan filed appeals before the Supreme Court, contending that it was a new sovereign not bound by the liabilities of the former State of Dholpur unless it expressly recognized them. The question before the Court was Whether the State of Rajasthan is liable under Article 295(2) of the Constitution to refund advance export duties deposited with the former State of Dholpur, given that the liability arose before the merger of Dholpur into the United State of Rajasthan. Held: Appeals dismissed: The appeals are dismissed, affirming the liability of the State of Rajasthan to refund the advance export duty to the respondent. The Court considered Constitution of India: Provides that the Government of a Part B State is the successor of the Government of the corresponding Indian State regarding all property, assets, rights, liabilities, and obligations. Constitution of India: Continued existing laws subject to alteration or repeal by the new State, supporting the argument that liabilities under old laws persisted. M/s. Dalmia Dadri Cement Co. Ltd. vs The Commissioner of Income-tax (Distinguished): Established that Covenants are acts of State and not directly enforceable, but their provisions can serve as evidence of the new State's intention to assume liabilities if subsequent conduct supports it. Maharaja Shree Umaid Mill Limited vs Union of India (Distinguished): Distinguished because in that case, a new competent law explicitly negated the recognition of old agreements, whereas no such law existed in the present case. Rajasthan Administration Ordinance No. 1 of 1949: Continued existing laws of old States and construed references to old Rulers as references to the new Government, indicating an intention to assume liabilities. Act of State doctrine: Covenants between sovereigns are acts of State and not directly enforceable by citizens, but they provide evidence of the new sovereign's intent regarding liabilities. Applying those rules, On Whether the State of Rajasthan is liable under Article 295(2) of the Constitution to refund advance export duties deposited with the former State of Dholpur, given that the liability arose before the merger of Dholpur into the United State of Rajasthan, the core question is whether the new sovereign (State of Rajasthan) recognized and assumed the liabilities of the former sovereign (State of Dholpur). Under the Act of State doctrine, the Covenants merging the states are not directly enforceable by citizens to claim rights against the new State. However, the Covenants serve as valuable evidence of the new State's intention to assume liabilities, particularly when viewed alongside the new State's subsequent conduct. In the present case, every merger involved a provision that existing laws of the merging states would continue in force until repealed or altered by the new State. The Rajasthan Administration Ordinance No. 1 of 1949 further continued these laws and substituted references to the old Ruler with the new Government. The continuance of old laws implies that the new State intended to respect rights flowing from those laws and assume the corresponding liabilities; otherwise, the continuance of laws would be meaningless. This situation distinguishes the present case from M/s. Dalmia Dadri Cement Co. Ltd., where the new State repealed old laws in merging states and applied the laws of one specific state, thereby negating recognition of other liabilities. It also distinguishes the present case from Maharaja Shree Umaid Mill Limited, where a new competent law explicitly negated the recognition of an old agreement. In the present case, no competent law was passed by the new State to repeal the old laws or negate the liability for the refund of advance export duty. Therefore, the combination of the Covenant provisions and the continuance of old laws constitutes sufficient recognition by the new State of the liabilities of the former State of Dholpur. Consequently, the State of Rajasthan is bound by the liability to refund the advance export duty under Article 295(2) of the Constitution. The State of Rajasthan is liable to refund the advance export duty as it recognized and assumed the liabilities of the former State of Dholpur through the continuance of laws and Covenant provisions.
reference_summary:
In 1947, the Dholpur State acceded to the Dominion of India.
Later on, it was merged with other States and as a result of that merger, the Matsya Union was formed on March 18, 1948.
One of the provisions of the merger agreement was that the existing laws in the Covenanting States were to be continued till such time as they were modified or repealed by the new State and that all the assets and liabilities of the Covenanting States were taken over by the new State.
Later on, the Matsya Union was merged with the United State of Rajasthan which had come into existence from April 7, 1949.
A similar provision with regard to the recognition of the liabilities of the Covenanting States by the new State was also provided.
On January 26, 1950, Part B State of Rajasthan came into existence.
In the four appeals the respondents secured permits from the Dholpur State for the export of certain commodities and they had to pay export duties in advance.
As the respondents could not export the full quantity for which they had secured permits they asked the appellant to refund the excess export duty and when the latter refused to do so, filed suits for refund of the same with interest.
The defence taken up by the appellant was that it was not bound by any liability which might have arisen against the former State of Dholpur.
It was a new Sovereign and was not bound by any liability of the former State of Dholpur unless it chose to recognise the obligation but no such obligation was recognised in the present case.
One suit was dismissed by the trial court and other three were decreed.
The appeals of the State to the District Judge were substantially dismissed while the appeal in the first suit by the plaintiff was substantially allowed.
The State filed appeals to the High Court.
After referring the matter to the Full Bench, a Division Ben oh of the High Court dismissed the appeals filed by the State.
The Appellant came to this Court after obtaining certificate of fitness from the High Court.
The only question raised before this Court was about the liability of the State of Rajasthan under article 295(2) of the Constitution in respect of the obligations of the former State of Dholpur which came to be included in the State of Rajasthan.
Dismissing the appeals, Held, that the new State by continuing the old laws without change till they were repealed or altered, recognised that it was liable in the same way as the merging State would have been in any case.
Throughout the process of integration from 1948 to 1950, the new Sovereign must be taken to have recognised the rights of the subjects and undertaken the liabilities 175 of the old State.
So under article 295(2) of the Constitution, the State of Rajasthan was liable to meet the liabilities of all old States which eventually were merged into it.
Moreover, there was nothing to show that the right to claim the refund was taken away by any law competently passed.
M/s Dalmia Dadri Cement Co. Limited vs The Commissioner of Income tax [1959], S.C.R. 729 and Maharaja Shree Umaid Mill Limited vs Union of India, A.I.R. 1953, S.C. 953 referred to.

prediction: Tata Consultancy Engineers (TCE), a service industry and division of Tata Sons Limited, was involved in an industrial dispute with the Tata Consultant Employees Union regarding wage scales and benefits. The Union served a Charter of Demands in July 1974, seeking upward revision of wage scales, dearness allowance, and removal of the Efficiency Bar. Conciliation proceedings failed, and the State Government referred the dispute to the Industrial Tribunal, Maharashtra, under Section 10(1)(d) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The Tribunal, in its award dated 20 December 1978, revised the wage scales by incorporating flat increases into the structure of the scales (Rs. 150 for Draughtsmen and Rs. 100 for others) and made the revision retrospective from 1 January 1976. The Tribunal rejected the Union's claim for a dearness allowance linked to the cost of living index, maintaining a fixed percentage scheme. On 22 December 1978, the Union applied under Rule 31 of the Industrial Disputes (Bombay) Rules, 1957, claiming an accidental omission in the award regarding the grant of a flat increase to 'each employee'. The Tribunal accepted the application, ordering a corrigendum to add the words 'to each employee' after the flat increase figures, effectively granting an additional ad hoc increase to individual workmen on top of the revised scales. TCE filed Civil Appeal No. 2299 of 1979 challenging the retrospectivity of the wage scales and the validity of the amendment order dated 22 December 1978. The Union filed Civil Appeal No. 2300 of 1979 challenging the rejection of their claim for a cost-of-living-linked dearness allowance. The Supreme Court heard both appeals by special leave. The question before the Court was Whether the Industrial Tribunal acted within its jurisdiction under Rule 31 of the Industrial Disputes (Bombay) Rules, 1957, in amending its award to grant a flat ad hoc increase to individual employees, or whether such amendment constituted a substantive modification of the award beyond the scope of correcting a clerical error; and Whether the Industrial Tribunal was justified in rejecting the workmen's claim for a dearness allowance linked to the cost of living index in favor of a fixed percentage scheme. Held: Appeals dismissed: Both Civil Appeal No. 2299 of 1979 and Civil Appeal No. 2300 of 1979 are dismissed in accordance with the majority opinion, upholding the original award and the Tribunal's order dated 22 December 1978. The Court considered Industrial Disputes (Bombay) Rules, 1957: The court analyzed whether the Tribunal's order correcting the award fell within the limited jurisdiction to correct clerical mistakes or accidental slips, or if it constituted a substantive modification of the award. Industrial Disputes Act, 1947: Cited as the statutory basis under which the State Government referred the industrial dispute to the Industrial Tribunal for adjudication. Consent cannot confer jurisdiction: The court held that even if the appellant submitted to the Tribunal's decision, consent cannot validate an order that is beyond the Tribunal's jurisdiction. Scope of Rule 31 correction: The court defined the principle that Rule 31 allows correction only of clerical mistakes or accidental slips, not errors requiring modification of conscious adjudication on issues. The Hindustan Times Ltd., New Delhi vs Their Workmen (Referred): Cited by the workmen to support the argument that dearness allowance should be on a sliding scale linked to the cost of living index rather than fixed. Constitution of India: Mentioned in the context of the standard for interference by the Supreme Court in special leave appeals. Applying those rules, On Whether the Industrial Tribunal acted within its jurisdiction under Rule 31 of the Industrial Disputes (Bombay) Rules, 1957, in amending its award to grant a flat ad hoc increase to individual employees, or whether such amendment constituted a substantive modification of the award beyond the scope of correcting a clerical error, rule 31 of the Industrial Disputes (Bombay) Rules, 1957, grants the Tribunal jurisdiction to correct clerical mistakes or errors arising from accidental slips or omissions. The scope of Rule 31 is strictly limited to clerical corrections and does not permit the modification of conscious adjudication on substantive issues. The original award focused on revising the wage scales by incorporating flat increases into the structure of the scales themselves, rather than granting ad hoc increases to individual employees. The financial burden calculated in the original award (approx. Rs. 5 lakhs) was based on the restructuring of wage scales, not on an additional flat increase to every individual employee. The amendment order added the words 'to each employee' to the flat increase figures, effectively creating a second, separate increase for individuals on top of the revised scales. This amendment altered the substantive relief granted and increased the financial burden beyond what was adjudicated in the original award. The Tribunal's reliance on Exhibit C 51 to prove intent for individual increases was erroneous, as that document merely presented hypothetical trial figures for various scenarios, none of which were adopted in the final award. The amendment effectively constituted a supplementary award granting new relief, which falls outside the jurisdiction of Rule 31. The appellant's consent to the amendment does not confer jurisdiction on the Tribunal to act beyond its statutory powers. The majority holds that the Tribunal committed a jurisdictional error by modifying the substantive award under the guise of correcting a clerical error. The amendment order dated 22nd December 1978 is invalid as it exceeds the Tribunal's jurisdiction under Rule 31 by substantively modifying the award rather than correcting a clerical error. On Whether the Industrial Tribunal was justified in rejecting the workmen's claim for a dearness allowance linked to the cost of living index in favor of a fixed percentage scheme, the workmen contend that dearness allowance should be linked to the cost of living index, citing precedents like The Hindustan Times Ltd. vs Their Workmen. Linking dearness allowance to the cost of living index is not a universal mandatory rule in all industrial disputes. The Tribunal has the discretion to determine the appropriate method for dearness allowance based on the specific facts and financial capacity of the employer. The Tribunal found that the appellant's financial capacity could not sustain the burden of a slab system or index-linked allowance combined with the revised wage scales. The award represents a composite and balanced arrangement integrating revised wage scales, increments, and a fixed percentage dearness allowance (10% of basic wage). The revised basic wages result in a consequential increase in the dearness allowance, providing sufficient relief to the workmen. Altering the dearness allowance structure would require reopening the entire award and reconsidering the financial basis upon which it was made. The Tribunal's decision to maintain the fixed percentage scheme was reasonable and within its jurisdiction. The Tribunal was justified in rejecting the claim for a cost-of-living-linked dearness allowance, as the fixed percentage scheme was part of a balanced award consistent with the employer's financial capacity.

Dismissing the appeals by special leave, the Court. ^ HELD: Per Pathak, J. (Krishna Iyer and Chinnappa Reddy, JJ.
concurring) (1) Having regard to the financial capacity of M/s. Tata Consulting Engineers, the appellant, and the material on the record and the various other considerations which prevailed with the Tribunal, the granting of revised wage scales is in order.
Although the wage scales were introduced as long ago as 1973 they were maintained at that level except for a slight revision some time thereafter.
No dearness allowance was paid until the beginning of 1977 and the house rent allowance also was introduced about that time.
The cost of living had gone on increasing from 1972 onwards and the dearness allowance and house rent allowances made no appreciable impact in neutralising the increasing cost.
During all these years, the appellant had continued to enjoy increasing profits; nonetheless the emoluments received by the workmen did not receive the impress of the appellant 's growing prosperity.
The Charter of Demands was presented by the Union in July, 1974 and when conciliation proceedings failed the State Government made a reference to the Industrial Tribunal in 1975.
The several considerations which prevailed with the Tribunal giving retrospectivity to the revised pay scales and referred to by it cannot be ignored.
[174C G] (2) It is not a universal rule that the dearness allowance should in all cases be correlated with the cost of living index.
The Tribunal, in the present case, considered the matter and found it sufficient and in accord with justice that the wage scales should be restructured with suitable increments provided therein.
It noted that dearness allowance was being granted by the appellant at 10% of the salary subject to a minimum of Rs. 50/ and house rent allowance at 30% of the basic salary.
Having regard to the not inconsiderable improvement in the level of the basic wage, it observed that there would be a consequent increase in the dearness allowance and house rent allowance.
In view of the increase so secured, the Tribunal rejected the suggestion that a slab system should be introduced in the dearness allowance or that there should be any other modification of the principle on which dearness allowance was being presently granted.
It declared that the cumulative effect of an im 167 proved wage structure together with dearness allowance operating on a slab system would throw an impossible burden of about Rs. 1 crore on the financial capacity of the appellant.
It was open to the Tribunal to adopt the position which it did.
If the dearness allowance is linked with the cost of living index the whole award will have to be reopened and the entire basis on which it has been made will have to be reconsidered.
The award is a composite document in which the several elements of increased wage scales, larger increments longer span of 20 years for earning increments, dearness allowance at 10% of the basic wage, besides several other benefits, have been integrated into a balanced arrangement in keeping with what the Tribunal has found to be the financial capacity of the appellant.
It is not possible to maintain one part of the award and supersede another.
[179 E F] The Hindustan Times Ltd, New Delhi vs Their Workmen, [1964] 1 SCR 234, 247 and Bengal Chemical & Pharmaceutical Works Limited vs its Workmen; , , distinguished.
(3) The jurisdiction given to the Tribunal by rule 31 of the Industrial Disputes (Bombay) Rules, 1957, is closely circumscribed.
It is only a clerical mistake or error which can be corrected and the clerical mistake or error must arise from an accidental slip or omission in the award.
An accidental slip or omission implies that something was intended and contrary to that intention what should not have been included has been included or what should have been included has been omitted.
It must be a mistake or error amenable to clerical correction only.
It must not be a mistake or error which calls for rectification by modification of the conscious adjudication on the issues involved.
[175 A C] Per contra The order of 22nd December, 1978 is invalid so far as it amends paragraph 23 of the original award.
The amendment has resulted in the Tribunal making, as it were, a supplementary award, whereby a further relief is being granted beyond that granted in the original award.
The original award was completed and signed by the Tribunal, and it cannot be reopened now except for the limited purpose of Rule 31.
In travelling outside and beyond the terms of the original award, the Tribunal has committed a jurisdictional error.
The evidence contained in the award throughout provides incontrovertible proof that this flat increase (ad hoc) was never originally intended in the award.
There was only one increase contemplated in the award, in paragraph 23 of the award and it is more than plain that the increase was the one incorporated in the revised pay scales pertaining to different categories.
No second flat increase was envisaged at all.
The amendment made by the Tribunal has the effect of providing a second increase, this time to each individual workmen.
If, as the Tribunal has stated in the amendment order.
the increase in paragraph 23 was intended to apply to each individual workmen, there is nothing in the body of the award to form the foundation on which the actual figures in the restructured pay scales can be made to rest.
There will be no explanation why the initial start of the revised pay scales has been increased by Rs. 150/ in the case of the category of Draughtsmen and Rs. 100/ in the case of other categories.
Considering the fitment of the workmen in the revised scales, it was stated in the award that workman found drawing a salary less than the beginning of the grade would be stepped up to the beginning of the grade and if his pay fell between two steps in the reclassified pay scales the 168 basic pay was to be fixed at the step higher in the revised scale.
Further the award was made on the basis that the overall financial load according to paragraph 33 of the award would be to the tune of about Rs. 5 lakhs.
It was that figure which the Tribunal had in mind against the backdrop of the gross annual figures when it made the revised pay scales retrospective from 1st January, 1976.
[176 D G, 177A, 178 D F] The statement, Exhibit C 51 afforded an indication merely of what the additional financial load would be if a flat increase was given to the individual workmen on the alternative basis set forth therein.
None of the alternatives actually adopted by the Tribunal, because when the award was made the Tribunal proceeded instead to restructure the wage scales by the addition of Rs. 150/ in the case of the category of Draughtsmen and of Rs. 100/ in the case of other categories to the initial pay in the wage scales pertaining to these categories.
The addition was integrated as a feature of the wage scales, it was not regarded as an addition to the pay of each individual workmen.
[178A C] It is an accepted principle that consent by a party cannot confer jurisdiction on a court.
What is without jurisdiction will remain so.
[178 E F] Per O. C. Reddy, J. (Majority view, Iyer and Reddy, JJ.) The order dated December 22, 1978 of the Industrial Tribunal which purports to correct the award dated December 20, 1978 cannot be considered in effect to be a fresh award and it is in order.
The omission of the words "to each employee" after the figure Rs. 150/ and again after the figure Rs. 100/ was clearly an accidental slip or omission which the Tribunal was entitled to correct.
The application for the correction was made immediately, that is to say, two days after the Award, while iron was still hot or when everything must have been fresh to the minds of the Tribunal.
Even the endorsement made on the application by the Advocate for the Company to the effect "submitted to whatever this honourable Tribunal desires to do, does not indicate that the Company had any objection to the award being corrected as sought by the employees union.
On the other hand the endorsement reads as if there was tacit agreement on the part of the Company to the correction sought by the union; it cannot possibly be doubted that an Industrial Tribunal deciding upon the wage scales of the employees of an establishment would have full liberty to propose ad hoc increase of salaries as part of the revision of pay scales, not can it be doubted that fitment into the revised pay scales is certainly a part of the revision of pay scales.
This is elementary and fundamental to the jurisdiction of the Industrial Tribunal in revising wage scales.
If without any flat or ad hoc increase of salary the workmen were to be fitted into revised scales of pay, it would, obviously, result in serious anomalous situations.
In the case of several senior employees, the revised scale would yield but a very small and almost a token increase in the size of the pay packet whereas the junior employees would get a large benefit.
While workmen raising industrial disputes for revision of wage scales are certainly minded about their future prospects in the matter of wages, they, surely would be more concerned with the immediate benefit accruing to them.
That was why the Industrial Tribunal thought that all round flat increase of Rs. 150/ in the case of Draughtsmen and Rs. 100/ in the case of other workmen to each employee was called for.

In the instant case, the Tribunal has given satisfactory reasons for adopting a different mode.

prediction: The appellant occupied premises owned by the Bombay City Weavers Cooperative Limited, which had previously obtained an ejectment decree against the respondent, who was the monthly tenant of the premises. On February 9, 1965, the appellant and the respondent executed a written agreement described as a 'leave and licence' for a period of five years, from September 1, 1965, to August 31, 1970. The agreement designated the respondent as the 'licensor' and the appellant as the 'licensee', granting the appellant permission to use the premises for workshop business only. The agreement stipulated that the licensee could work for twenty hours, subject to local authority rules, and prohibited residential use or any other purpose. The agreement reserved to the licensor the right to enter and inspect the premises at any time and required the licensee to pay monthly 'compensation' of Rs. 225, while the licensor remained responsible for paying rent to the owner. The agreement provided that the licensor could terminate the agreement if the licensee failed to pay compensation for two months or put up a false claim of tenancy. The respondent filed ejectment proceedings against the appellant under Section 41 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel Rooms and Lodging Houses Act, 1947, after the agreement expired. The Court of Small Causes, Bombay, found that the appellant was a licensee and not a sub-tenant, and passed a decree for eviction. The High Court of Bombay initially allowed the appellant's special civil application under Article 227 of the Constitution but was directed by the Supreme Court in a previous appeal (Civil Appeal No. 2181 of 1977) to reconsider the matter in light of the decision in D.H. Maniar vs Waman Laxman Kudav. Upon reconsideration, the High Court disallowed the special civil application, affirming the trial court's finding that the appellant was a licensee and upholding the eviction order. The appellant filed the present civil appeal by special leave to the Supreme Court challenging the High Court's order. The question before the Court was Whether the agreement between the parties created a lease (tenancy) or merely a leave and licence; and Whether the High Court was justified in not interfering with the trial court's finding that the appellant was a licensee under Article 227 of the Constitution. Held: Appeal dismissed: The appeal is dismissed, and the appellant is directed to deliver vacant possession of the premises by March 31, 1988, subject to filing an undertaking within three weeks. The Court considered Transfer of Property Act, 1882: Defines a lease as a transfer of a right to enjoy property, used to distinguish it from a licence which does not transfer an interest. Bombay Rents, Hotel Rooms and Lodging Houses Act, 1947: Provides the mechanism for ejecting a person occupying property by permission after such permission is determined or withdrawn. D.H. Maniar and others vs Waman Laxman Kudav (Relied on): Held that a person continuing in possession after the termination or revocation of a licence is a trespasser and does not acquire the status of a tenant under Section 15A of the Bombay Rent Act. Associated Hotels of India Ltd. vs R.N. Kapoor (Relied on): Established that the decisive consideration in determining whether an agreement is a lease or licence is the intention of the parties, and that a lease involves a transfer of interest. Intention of Parties: The court applied the principle that the substance of the document and the intention of the parties, rather than the form, determine the legal character of the agreement. Constitution of India: The court considered the scope of the High Court's supervisory jurisdiction, holding that it should not interfere if the trial court's view is plausible and possible. Applying those rules, On Whether the agreement between the parties created a lease (tenancy) or merely a leave and licence, the distinction between a lease and a licence depends on the intention of the parties, ascertained from the substance of the document and surrounding circumstances. A lease involves a transfer of an interest in immovable property, whereas a licence merely grants permission to use the property without transferring any interest. The agreement in question is explicitly titled 'leave and licence' and identifies the parties as licensor and licensee. The agreement imposes significant restrictions on the appellant's use, limiting it to workshop business for twenty hours and prohibiting residential use. The agreement reserves to the licensor the right to enter and inspect the premises at any time, indicating that exclusive possession was not transferred. The payment is termed 'compensation' rather than rent, and the licensor remains liable for the rent to the owner. These terms negate the intention to create a tenancy or transfer an interest in the property. The agreement expired on August 31, 1970, and the appellant continued in possession thereafter without a subsisting agreement. Following the precedent in D.H. Maniar, a person continuing in possession after the termination of a licence is a trespasser and does not acquire tenant status. The trial court's finding that the appellant was a licensee is a plausible view based on the evidence and the document's terms. The agreement created a leave and licence, not a lease; the appellant is a licensee liable for eviction. On Whether the High Court was justified in not interfering with the trial court's finding that the appellant was a licensee under Article 227 of the Constitution, the High Court exercises supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227 to correct errors apparent on the face of the record. Where two views are possible and the trial court has taken one plausible view, the High Court should not interfere merely because another view is attractive. The trial court's conclusion that the appellant was a licensee was a possible and plausible interpretation of the agreement. There was no error apparent on the face of the record that would justify interference under Article 227. The High Court was justified in affirming the trial court's decision.

Sub section (7) of section 63 of the empowers the State Transport Authority, for the purpose of promoting tourism, to grant permits valid for the whole or any part of India, in respect of such number of tourist vehicles as the Central Government may in respect of that State specify in this behalf.
A proviso to that sub section, introduced by section 24 of the Amending Act of 1978 laid down that preference shall be given to applications for permits from (i) the India Tourism Development Corporation; (iii) a State Tourism Development Corporation; (iii) a State Tourist Department, and (iv) operators of tourist cars, or travel agents, approved in this behalf by the Central Government.
There were as many as 495 applications before the Karnataka State Transport Authority for the grant of 14 All India Tourist Vehicle permits.
By its proceedings dated April 30, 1984, the Authority granted 11 permits to the Karnataka State Tourism Development Corporation, one to the Indian Tourism Development Corporation and two to the Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation.
1009 On appeals being preferred, the Karnataka State Transport Appellate Tribunal, by its order dated February 28, 1985 set aside the grant of two permits in favour of the Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation, three out of eleven permits to the Karnataka State Tourism Development Corporation, and instead granted three permits to private operators and increased the number of permits granted to the Indian Tourism Development Corporation from one to three, on the premises that in view of the rule of preference enunciated by the proviso to section 63(7) the applications from the non preferred category had to be excluded as the number of applications from the applicants who were required to be given preference exceeded the number of permits to be granted.
Though some of the appellants before the Tribunal had better expertise, experience and resources they did not succeed.
The High Court rejected the writ petitions on the ground that the rule of preference contained in the proviso to section 63(7) contemplated exclusion of the 'non preferred ' class, if sufficient number of applicants from the preferred classes were available.
In these appeals by special leave, it was contended for the appellants that on a correct interpretation of the proviso to section 63(7) the preference became operative only if other things were equal.
It was also urged that the fourth sub clause of the proviso offended article 14 of the Constitution, and had to be struck down.
Allowing the appeals, the Court, ^ HELD: 1.1 The rule contained in the proviso to section 63(7) of the is a rule of preference and not a rule of exclusion, for it does not say that the permit shall be granted to the categories of operators specified therein.
The claims of eligible applicants must be considered on merits, applying the rule of preference whenever the claims are approximately equal.
The application of an applicant is not to be altogether excluded from consideration on the sole ground that another applicant is entitled to preference.
Though the proviso does not expressly refer to other things being equal, the principle is very much implicit in it.
[1015B E] 1.2 What has been said by this Court in Sher Singh vs Union of India; , , about preference in relation to section 47(1 H) applies mutatis mutandis to the preference contemplated by the proviso to section 63(7) in the instant case.
[1017C] 1010 2.1 Clause (iv) of the proviso to section 63(7) is arbitrary, unreasonable and unconstitutional.
There is no indication in it as to the manner in which the approval of the Central Government is to be sought and granted and the considerations which are expected to weigh with the Central Government.
It compels a tribunal, created by a statute for the purpose of considering rival claims and granting permits on merits, to give preference to persons securing the approval of the Executive Government.
To the extent the clause goes, it pre empts the decision of the designated tribunal by executive discretion.
[1017E G] 2.2 The clause provides for a preference not to operators of tourist vehicles but to operators of tourist cars and travel agents, though the permits to be granted are for tourist vehicles.
It is difficult to understand why preference should be given to operators of tourist cars in the matter of granting permits for tourist vehicles which may well be omnibuses required to travel long distances.
[1018B C] 2.3 The experience of running a tourist taxi cannot be said to be a better qualification than running a tourist bus when the question is of granting permits for tourist vehicles.
[1018C D] 3.
Having regard to the definitions of 'tourist vehicle ' and 'motor car ' contained in section 2(29 A) and section 2(16) respectively of the Act, the expression 'tourist cars ' cannot be said to mean 'tourist vehicles '.
While a tourist vehicle may include a motor car, a motor car, by definition, excludes an omnibus.
[1018D E] In the instant case, the State Transport Appellate Tribunal and the High Court have failed to consider the merits of the claims of the Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation and the private operators who did not get a certificate of approval from the Central Government, because of the rule of preference contained in proviso to section 63(7).

Minimum Wages Act, 1948: Mandates overtime payment for work in excess of the normal working day. Minimum Wages (Central) Rules, 1950: Defines the normal working day for an adult as 9 hours and stipulates that the working day, inclusive of rest intervals, shall not spread over more than 12 hours. Minimum Wages (Central) Rules, 1950: Sets the overtime rate at double the ordinary rate and limits the maximum weekly work hours to 48. Factories Act, 1948: Used to contrast with the Minimum Wages Act, noting that the latter does not mandate compulsory rest intervals breaking up work hours, allowing for variable recess in tidal dock work. Section 13 of the Act and Rule 24 of the Rules define the 'normal working day' as 9 hours of work for an adult. Rule 24(2) allows the working day to spread over a maximum of 12 hours, inclusive of specified intervals of rest. An 'interval of rest' is a predetermined period where the employee is not required to display physical activity or sustained attention, distinct from inaction due to lack of work. Section 14 mandates overtime pay only for work performed in excess of the normal working day (9 hours). Rule 25 limits total weekly work to 48 hours, averaging 8 hours per day over a six-day week. The Corporation is a company incorporated under the Companies Act, with the primary object of preserving traditional arts and crafts, providing training to artisans, and marketing their products. The Corporation has suffered financial losses and maintains only administrative staff in production centers, employing no permanent craftsmen. The petitioners filed a petition under Article 32 of the Constitution seeking enforcement of the fundamental right to 'equal pay for equal work' compared to regular carpenters in Government service. Alternatively, the petitioners sought payment of minimum wages prescribed by the Deputy Commissioner for Class IV Government employees under Exhibit P.2 dated March 20, 1986. The petitioners also sought regularization of their services with benefits such as pension and gratuity. The Corporation contended that the petitioners are industrial workmen treated as construction workers, paid minimum wages applicable to the construction industry, and provided with tools and uniforms. The Corporation stated that there are no regular employees in the petitioners' category within its establishment, so the question of parity with regular employees does not arise internally. The petitioners are covered under the Bonus Act and the Employees' Provident Fund Act. The question before the Court was Whether the petitioners, employed by the Himachal Pradesh State Handicrafts Corporation, are entitled to claim 'equal pay for equal work' in comparison to regular carpenters in Government service; and Whether the petitioners are entitled to the minimum wages prescribed by the Deputy Commissioner for Class IV Government employees under Exhibit P.2. Held: Petition dismissed: The petition is dismissed as the petitioners are not entitled to equal pay with government servants due to being employed by a different establishment, nor are they entitled to the minimum wages prescribed for government employees under Exhibit P.2. The Court considered Constitution of India: Article 39(d) contains the Directive Principle of 'equal pay for equal work', which has been read into Articles 14 and 16 as a constitutional goal enforceable via Article 32. Meva Ram Kanojia vs All India Institute of Medical Sciences (Relied on): Held that the principle of equal pay for equal work cannot be invoked invariably and that discrimination must be within the same establishment owned by the same management. State of U.P. vs J.P. Chaurasia (Relied on): Clarified that equal pay for equal work has no mechanical application and allows reasonable classification based on merit, experience, and seniority. Federation of All India Customs and Central Excise Stenographers vs Union of India (Relied on): Established that equal pay depends on the nature, reliability, and responsibility of work, not just volume, and that bona fide administrative value judgments are permissible. Applying those rules, On Whether the petitioners, employed by the Himachal Pradesh State Handicrafts Corporation, are entitled to claim 'equal pay for equal work' in comparison to regular carpenters in Government service, the principle of 'equal pay for equal work' is derived from Article 39(d) and read into Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. Judicial precedents establish that this principle is not mechanically applicable and permits reasonable classification based on merit, experience, and responsibility. A critical limitation is that the discrimination complained of must exist within the same establishment owned by the same management. The petitioners are employed by the Himachal Pradesh State Handicrafts Corporation, a distinct entity incorporated under the Companies Act. The petitioners seek parity with carpenters in Government service, which constitutes a different establishment with different management. Comparison of wages across different establishments or different masters is not permissible under the principle of equal pay for equal work. Furthermore, the Corporation has no regular employees in the petitioners' category, meaning there is no internal discrimination within the same establishment. The nature of the work involves craftsmanship where accuracy, dexterity, and responsibility vary, requiring expert evaluation rather than mere comparison of job titles or volume of work. Therefore, the petitioners cannot enforce the right to equal pay against the Government or claim parity with government servants. The claim for equal pay for equal work is rejected because the petitioners are employed by a different establishment than the government servants they seek parity with, and no internal discrimination exists within the Corporation. On Whether the petitioners are entitled to the minimum wages prescribed by the Deputy Commissioner for Class IV Government employees under Exhibit P.2, the petitioners alternatively claim minimum wages as prescribed by the Deputy Commissioner under Exhibit P.2 dated March 20, 1986. Exhibit P.2 was issued by the Deputy Commissioner exercising powers under the H.P. Financial Rules. The scope of Exhibit P.2 is explicitly limited to skilled and unskilled workers in Class IV employees in Government service. The petitioners are employees of the Himachal Pradesh State Handicrafts Corporation, not Government service employees. The H.P. Financial Rules and Exhibit P.2 have not been extended to apply to employees of the Corporation. The Corporation currently treats the petitioners as construction workers and pays them the minimum wages admissible to such workmen. The Court lacks the authority to direct the Corporation to apply rates prescribed under Exhibit P.2 unless the Government formally extends the applicability of those rules to the Corporation's employees. The claim for minimum wages under Exhibit P.2 is rejected as the order is inapplicable to Corporation employees.

However, book entries alone are insufficient if the entity holding the accounts cannot honor the transfer. If the entity is a banking company or has sufficient overdraft facilities, it can honor the instructions, making the book entries valid delivery. Sub section (4) of section 5 of the Taxation on Income (Investigation Commission) Act, 1947, does not deal with the same class of persons as are said to have been grouped together in subsection (1) of section 5 of the Act as persons who to a substantial extent evaded payment of taxation on income.
On a plain reading of the section it is clear that sub section (4) of section 5 is not limited only to persons who made extraordinary profits and to all persons who may have evaded payment of taxation on income irrespective of whether the evaded profits are substantial or insubstantial and therefore the scope of sub section (4) of section 5 is different from the scope of sub section (1) of section 5 both in extent and range.
Sub section (4) of section 5 of the Act, obviously deals with the same class of persons who fall within the ambit of section 34 of the Indian Income tax Act and are dealt with in sub section (1) of that section and whose income can be caught by the proceeding under that section.
It is not possible to hold that all such persons who evaded payment of income tax and do not truly disclose all particulars or material facts necessary for their assessment and against whom a, report is made under sub section (4) of section 5 of the impugned 449 Act by themselves form a class distinct from those who evade payment of income tax and come within the ambit of section 34 of the Indian Income tax Act.
Both section 34 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1.922, and subsection (4) of section 5 of the Taxation on Income (Investigation Commission) Act, 1947, deal with all persons who have similar characteristics and similar properties, the common characteristics being that they are persons who have not truly disclosed their income and have evaded payment of taxation on income.
The procedure prescribed by the Taxation on Income (Investigation Commission) Act, 1947, is substantially more prejudicial and more drastic to the assessee than the procedure under the Indian Income tax Act (XI of 1922).
Held, therefore that sub section (4) of section 5 and the procedure prescribed by the impugned Act in so far as it affects the persons proceeded against under that sub section being a piece of discriminatory legislation offends against the provisions of article 14 of the Constitution and is thus void and unenforceable.

One of the petitions was dismissed by a learned single judge of the High Court and the said petitions filed an appeal before a Division Bench of the High Court.
During the pendency of the appeal 233 and the writ petition,the Supreme Court by its order dated April 18, 1985 decided the case of Union of India vs Rajnikant Bros. holding that there was no requirement of diversification of exports as a condition for the grant of Export Houses Certificates in the Import Export Policy for the year 1978 79 but the grantee of Additional Licences were not only prohibited from importing items which were excluded in the Export Policy 1978 79 but also from importing items excluded under the Import Policy prevailing at the time import.
The High Court decided the cases of the petitioners in accordance with the decision of this Court in Union of India vs Rajnikant Bros. Purusant to the decision of the Bombay High Court petitioners were granted Export House Certificates and Additional Import Licences which were valid for 12 months, with the same condition as provided by this Court in its order dated April18, 1985 in the case of Rajnikant.
However, the petitioners were not able to make imports under the said licences till 31st March,1988.On 1.4.1988, the Government of India issued a revised Export and Import Policy for the period 1988 91.Under Para 215 of the said revised policy certain flexibilities were granted in the matter of imports to the grantees of Additional Import Licences.
However, under para 218(10) of the said revised Policy the holdersof the Additional Import Licences issuedprior to 1.4.1988 were made ineligible for the benefit of flexibilities in import as contained in para 215(4).
Since ,the petitioners were holding licences issued prior to 1.4.1988 they could not avail the flexibilities in import as contained in Para 215 of the 1988 91 Policy.
Consequently, they filed writ petitions in this Court challenging the validity of para218(10) of the 1988 91 Policy contending (i) that all the Export Houses who were granted Additional Licences constitute at single class and their classification on the basis of date or on the basis of period of exports has no connection with the object sought to be achieved by the 1988 91 policy; (ii) that Para 218(10) of 1988 91 Policy arbitrarily discriminates between Export Houses who were issued Additional Licences prior to 1.4.1988 since the benefits ofPara 214 of 1988 91 Policy were conferred only on the latter; (iii) that in view of the judgement of this Court in C.Naveenchandra and Co. vs Union of India, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 989 the petitioners should be treated at par with the grantees of Additional Licences under the Export Policy for the subsequent years and since there has been relaxation in the matter of policy of canalisation of imports under Para 215(4) in respect Additional Licences granted to Export Houses under the 1988 91 Policy, the petitioners were also entitled to a similar relaxation.

The right to equality guaranteed under Article 14 ensures equality amongst equals and its aim is to protect persons similarly placed against discriminatory treatment.
